outline: Economic growth versus economic development and their measurement

modules.title: Growth, Development and Planning
modules.html:
1.1 Growth versus development

Economic growth is a sustained increase in real national output or real income per head; it is quantitative and measured by the rate of growth of real GDP. Economic development is growth plus structural and institutional change that improves welfare: rising per-capita income, reduced poverty and inequality, better health and education, industrialisation and modern institutions. Growth without development is possible, as when oil revenue raises GDP while poverty, unemployment and inequality persist. Development is measured with the Human Development Index (income, life expectancy, education), poverty headcounts and the Gini coefficient.

1.2 Characteristics and problems of developing economies

  • Low per-capita income and widespread poverty; high dependence on primary production.
  • Rapid population growth and a high dependency ratio.
  • Low savings and investment; capital deficiency and a vicious circle of poverty.
  • High unemployment and under-employment; low productivity and human capital.
  • Dualistic economies: modern urban sector alongside traditional subsistence sector.
  • Weak infrastructure, technological dependence, unfavourable terms of trade, heavy debt, and institutional weaknesses including corruption.

1.3 Meaning and types of planning

Economic planning is the deliberate government effort to coordinate economic decisions over a period in order to achieve stated targets. Types: comprehensive versus partial planning; indicative (persuasive, as in a mixed economy) versus imperative (compulsory, as in a command economy); short-term (annual budget), medium-term (rolling plan, 3–5 years) and long-term (perspective plan of 15–20 years).

Objectives: raising national income and per-capita income, full employment, balanced regional and sectoral development, price stability, reduced inequality, diversification, self-reliance and efficient use of scarce resources.

1.4 Planning in Nigeria and reasons for failure

Nigeria has used the 1962–68, 1970–74, 1975–80 and 1981–85 development plans, rolling plans, Vision 2010/2020, NEEDS, the Transformation Agenda, ERGP and successive medium-term national development plans. Plans often failed because of unreliable data, over-ambitious targets, dependence on volatile oil revenue, political instability and policy discontinuity, corruption and leakages, shortage of skilled manpower, weak implementation and monitoring, and excessive dependence on foreign aid and imported inputs.

examples.q: Distinguish between economic growth and economic development with a Nigerian example.
examples.a: Growth is a rise in real output, for example real GDP expanding by 3% because of higher crude oil production. Development requires that this be accompanied by falling poverty and unemployment, better schools, health care and infrastructure and a more diversified economy. Nigeria has often recorded oil-driven growth while human development indicators improved only slightly — growth without development.

examples.q: State three reasons why development plans fail in developing countries.
examples.a: (i) Inadequate and unreliable statistical data leading to unrealistic targets. (ii) Insufficient and unstable finance, especially where revenue depends on volatile commodity prices. (iii) Weak implementation capacity, political instability and corruption, which divert plan resources.

modules.title: Unemployment, Wages and Human Capital
modules.html:
2.1 Unemployment

Unemployment exists when people who are willing and able to work at the prevailing wage cannot find jobs.

$$ \text{Unemployment rate} = \frac{\text{Number unemployed}}{\text{Labour force}} \times 100 $$

TypeCause
FrictionalTime spent moving between jobs
StructuralChange in the structure of demand or technology; skills mismatch
Cyclical (demand-deficient)Recession and fall in aggregate demand
SeasonalSeasonal nature of farming, tourism, construction
TechnologicalReplacement of labour by machines
ResidualDisability, age or personal factors
Disguised / under-employmentWorking below capacity or in low-productivity jobs

Effects: loss of output, poverty, crime and insecurity, waste of human capital, emigration and social unrest, loss of tax revenue.
Remedies: expansionary fiscal and monetary policy, promotion of small and medium enterprises, vocational and entrepreneurial education, agricultural modernisation, labour-intensive public works, employment information services, population control and improved security for investment.

2.2 Wages and the labour market

Nominal wage is money earnings; real wage is its purchasing power:

$$ \text{Real wage} = \frac{\text{Nominal wage}}{\text{Price index}} \times 100 $$

Wages differ because of skill and training, productivity, risk, elasticity of labour supply, trade union power, government legislation, immobility of labour and non-monetary advantages. Wage determination methods include collective bargaining, wage commissions, statutory minimum wages, productivity bargaining and arbitration.

Trade unions (craft, industrial, general, white-collar) seek higher wages, better conditions, job security and worker welfare. Weapons: negotiation, strike, work-to-rule, picketing, boycott; employers may use lock-out. Union strength depends on membership size, funds, leadership, level of employment and the elasticity of demand for the product.

2.3 Human capital and manpower planning

Human capital is the stock of skills, knowledge and health embodied in people. Investment in education, training, health and nutrition raises productivity, incomes and adaptability. Manpower planning forecasts the numbers and skills required in each sector and matches training programmes to them, reducing both graduate unemployment and skill shortages. Constraints include the brain drain, poor funding of education, mismatch between curricula and industry needs, and weak labour market data.

2.4 Reforms, poverty reduction and sustainability

Reform measures used in Nigeria include the Structural Adjustment Programme, deregulation, privatisation, banking consolidation, pension and tax reforms, subsidy reform and social investment programmes. Sustainable development meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs, requiring environmental protection, diversification away from depletable oil, and investment in renewable resources and human capital.

examples.q: A country has a labour force of 60 million with 9 million unemployed. Compute the unemployment rate.
Nominal wage rises from ₦60,000 to ₦75,000 while the price index rises from 100 to 150. What happens to the real wage?
examples.a: Real wage before = 60,000; after = (75,000/150) × 100 = ₦50,000. Although money wages rose by 25%, prices rose by 50%, so the real wage fell from ₦60,000 to ₦50,000 — the worker is worse off.

quiz.q: Economic growth is best measured by the rate of increase in:
quiz.solution: Growth refers to a sustained rise in real output, usually real GDP or real GDP per head.

quiz.q: Economic development differs from economic growth because development includes:
quiz.solution: Development combines rising output with poverty reduction, better health, education and institutional change.

quiz.q: The Human Development Index combines income with:
quiz.solution: HDI averages indicators of income, longevity and schooling to measure development.

quiz.q: A common characteristic of developing economies is:
quiz.solution: Their economies rely heavily on agriculture and mineral exports with low value added.

quiz.q: The vicious circle of poverty refers to:
options: Low income leading to low saving, low investment and low income
quiz.solution: Poverty limits saving and therefore investment, which keeps productivity and income low.

quiz.q: Indicative planning is typical of a:
quiz.solution: In mixed economies plans set targets and incentives without compelling private firms to comply.

quiz.q: A rolling plan is a form of:
quiz.solution: A rolling plan is a medium-term plan whose targets are updated each year in the light of performance.

quiz.q: Which is a major reason for the failure of development plans in Nigeria?
quiz.solution: Poor statistics, oil-dependent finance, policy discontinuity and corruption have repeatedly undermined plans.

quiz.q: Unemployment caused by a fall in aggregate demand during a recession is:
quiz.solution: Cyclical or demand-deficient unemployment moves with the trade cycle.

quiz.q: Unemployment resulting from a mismatch between workers' skills and available jobs is:
quiz.solution: Structural unemployment follows changes in technology or the pattern of demand.

quiz.q: If 6 million out of a labour force of 40 million are unemployed, the unemployment rate is:
Unemployment among farm workers during the dry season is:
quiz.solution: It arises from the seasonal pattern of agricultural activity.

quiz.q: Real wage is nominal wage adjusted for:
quiz.solution: Real wage measures purchasing power, so money wages are deflated by a price index.

quiz.q: If nominal wage rises by 20% while prices rise by 30%, the real wage:
quiz.solution: Prices rise faster than money wages, so purchasing power declines.

quiz.q: A trade union is strongest in wage bargaining when:
options: Demand for the firm's product is inelastic and membership is large
Members are unskilled and easily replaced
quiz.solution: Employers can pass higher wage costs on in prices, and a large, united membership makes strike threats credible.

quiz.q: An employers' response of closing the workplace during a dispute is a:
quiz.solution: A lock-out is the employer's counterpart of the strike.

quiz.q: Investment in education and health is described as investment in:
quiz.solution: It raises the productive capacity embodied in people, that is human capital.

quiz.q: Sustainable development means meeting present needs:
options: Without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs
quiz.solution: It requires balancing economic, social and environmental objectives over the long term.
